The question of whether ancient Greeks practiced human sacrifice is a matter of genuine scholarly debate, with sources offering conflicting conclusions. On one hand, d2 (Live Science) states that "textual references and archaeological remains indicate that the ancient Greeks, at times, practiced human sacrifice," citing a 3,000-year-old skeleton found at an altar dedicated to Zeus at Mount Lykaion [d2]. Similarly, d3 affirms that "the ancient Greeks practiced 'pharmakos,' whereby cripples, criminals, or slaves would be thrown off a cliff to ward off disaster" [d3], and d5 notes that "experts now believe that human sacrifice was practiced throughout the region during the Bronze Age into the Greek Dark Ages and possibly well beyond that" [d5]. On the other hand, d6 explicitly states that "the ancient Greeks are not believed to have practiced human sacrifice," even though the theme appears in their tragedies [d6]. d1 takes a more ambiguous position, suggesting that mythological references to sacrifice—such as the Iphigeneia story—"may be a vestigial memory of the abandonment and discrediting of the practice of human sacrifice among the Greeks" [d1]. Overall, while archaeological and textual evidence increasingly supports some degree of actual practice, particularly in earlier periods, a competing scholarly view holds that the Greeks did not practice it, and the debate remains unresolved [d2][d5][d6].
